title: Unequal Childhoods
text:
The sociologist Annette Lareau wanted to see, in close detail, how social class shapes the daily lives of children. In the 1990s, she and her research assistants interviewed many families in a city and suburbs in the northeastern United States and then chose twelve families with children around nine and ten years old, Black and white, middle class, working class and poor, for intensive observation.

The researchers visited each family about twenty times, often for hours, riding along to soccer games and church, sitting through dinners and homework, and sometimes staying overnight.

Lareau found two broad cultural logics of child rearing. Middle-class parents practiced what she called concerted cultivation. Their children's days were filled with organized activities, parents reasoned and negotiated with them, and they encouraged children to question adults and speak up to doctors and teachers. These children gained a sense of entitlement that served them well in institutions, but families were often exhausted and siblings had little free time.

Working-class and poor parents practiced what she called the accomplishment of natural growth. They provided love, food and safety and then let children organize their own play, often with cousins and neighbors. Parents gave directives rather than reasons. These children were more independent and inventive with their time, but more often showed a sense of constraint when dealing with schools and officials.
lesson: Both structure and freedom give children something valuable. Teach children to speak up to institutions, and also leave them time to play on their own.
source: Lareau, A. (2003). Unequal Childhoods: Class, Race, and Family Life. Berkeley: University of California Press.
caveat: The study is based on a small number of families observed in depth, so its patterns are illustrative rather than statistically representative.
